extracted.intended_audience: patent policymakers, patent examiners, patent attorneys, and IP practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical guidance for determining when claims that involve laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101, based on the Supreme Court's decision in Mayo v. Prometheus. Includes examples of routine/conventional steps that do not render a claim patentable and the USPTO three-step inquiry derived from the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are excluded from patent protection; they are basic tools of scientific and technological work and monopolization of those tools through patents might impede innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this exclusion as a foundational screening principle for subject-matter eligibility under §101. Examples given: laws like E=mc² or gravity cannot be patented; naturally occurring correlations (e.g., metabolite levels correlated with drug efficacy/toxicity) are similarly unpatentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: An application of a natural law is not patentable if its steps are routine/conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: An application of a natural law is not patentable if the steps used to apply the natural law involve well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by researchers in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims, identify whether claimed steps merely recite known, conventional techniques. If so, they do not transform an unpatentable law of nature into a patent-eligible invention. The Court applied this to the Prometheus claims (measuring metabolites, applying correlations, adjusting dosage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional features that add nothing specific to the natural law do not make the claim patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements or steps that add nothing specific to laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas—beyond what is well-understood, routine, and conventional—do not render the claim patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether extra claim language meaningfully integrates the natural principle into a practical application (i.e., adds 'significantly more'). Mere recitation of generic or conventional elements is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must do more than state the law and add the words 'apply it' ('significantly more')
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for an application of a natural law to be patentable, one must do more than simply state the law of nature while adding the words 'apply it.' The claimed invention must amount to 'significantly more' than the natural principle itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for transformative, inventive integration of the law into a specific, novel application rather than high-level or result-focused instructions. The absence of 'significantly more' supports ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional steps specified at a high level of generality cannot make a law patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Appending conventional steps, specified at a high level of generality, to laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas cannot make those subjects patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claimed steps are described at a high level of generality and are routine. Examples/anti-patterns provided: 'administering' that merely identifies an interested class of users (doctors); 'determining' that allows measurement 'through whatever process the doctor wishes' where such methods are well known; a step that merely tells a practitioner to consider results when making decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting a formula/idea to a particular technological environment is not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A prohibition against patenting abstract ideas cannot be circumvented by attempting to limit the use of the formula to a particular technological environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely place an abstract idea or law of nature into a field-specific context (e.g., targeting doctors treating a disease) without adding nonconventional, specific application elements should be treated as ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should not try to distinguish among laws of nature based on predicted interference with innovation; use a bright-line exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court concluded it is not institutionally well suited to make fine-grained judgments about which laws of nature will interfere significantly with innovation; therefore jurisprudence endorses a bright-line prohibition against patenting laws of nature, mathematical formulas, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ad hoc line-drawing that depends on speculative future harms/benefits across fields; instead apply the established exclusion and the 'significantly more' test to determine eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is distinct from patentability (novelty, non-obviousness, written description) and must be decided first
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between eligibility of a subject matter for patent protection and the patentability criteria (novelty, non-obviousness, and written description). Only patent-eligible subject matter is subject to the patentability criteria and the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine §101 eligibility before assessing novelty/non-obviousness. Relying solely on novelty or non-obviousness to screen laws of nature risks allowing monopolization of fundamental tools because undisclosed laws may not be defeated by prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO three-step inquiry for Mayo-derived subject-matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO guidance sets out a three-step inquiry: (1) Does the Mayo decision apply in principle? (Is the invention a process, i.e., an act or series of acts/steps?) (2) Does the patent application address a contentious subject matter? (Does it focus on use of a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or naturally occurring relation/correlation?) (3) Does the subject matter meet the requirements laid down under Mayo? (Do additional elements integrate the natural principle into the invention such that it is 'significantly more' than the natural principle itself?)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three questions as an examiner/practitioner checklist. For step (3), ask whether additional elements/steps 'integrate' the natural principle into a practical application and whether that integration is sufficient to be more than the principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relying solely on other statutory provisions (novelty/non-obviousness) to preserve eligibility is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: The government's proposed approach—treating any step beyond a statement of a law of nature as potentially patentable and relying on novelty, non-obviousness, and disclosure requirements to police overbroad claims—would render the law-of-nature exception a dead letter and create greater legal uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, do not collapse §101 into later patentability inquiries; maintain a §101 inquiry to prevent undue monopolization of fundamental tools and to provide clearer legal boundaries.
